passages.title: When the sun is folded up: the world undone
passages.tafsir:
These seven ayat are the opening of Sūrat al-Takwīr, a rapid sequence of "when…" clauses in which Allah dismantles, piece by piece, everything human beings have ever relied on as fixed: the sun, the stars, the mountains, their most prized wealth, the animal world, the seas, and finally the sorting of souls themselves. What binds them together is a single grammatical thread — each ayah is a conditional clause, a "when," and the answer to all of them is held back until later in the sūrah, beyond this passage, at ayah 14: "Every person will know what he has brought." Ibn Kathir calls that ayah "the conclusive response of the previous statements." In other words, the whole cascade of cosmic collapse exists to deliver one point: on that Day, nothing will remain standing except you and your deeds.

## A sūrah that makes you see the Day

Imam Ahmad recorded from Ibn 'Umar that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever wishes to look at the Day of Judgement as if he is seeing it with his own eyes, then let him read: 'When the sun is wound round' (81:1), and 'When the heaven is cleft asunder' (82:1), and 'When the heaven is split asunder' (84:1)." At-Tirmidhi also recorded this hadith.

This is the key to how the passage should be read. It is not a list of doctrines to memorise but a scene to witness. The Prophet ﷺ is telling us that reciting these ayat is the closest a person can come, in this life, to standing inside that Day and watching it happen.

## Ayah 1 — the folding of the sun

The word *kuwwirat* comes from *takwīr*, which in Arabic means to gather one part of a thing into another — to fold. Ibn Kathir notes that the same root gives us the folding of the turban (*'imāmah*) and the folding of clothes. So the image is startlingly physical: the sun, the great lamp of the world, will be folded up on itself like a garment, "then it will be rolled up and thrown away. When this is done to it, its light will go away."

The early authorities each caught a facet of this. Ibn 'Abbas said (in the report of Ali bin Abi Talhah), "it will be darkened," and in al-'Awfi's report, "it will go away." Qatadah said, "its light will go away." Sa'id bin Jubayr said it will sink in; Abu Salih said it will be thrown down. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that al-Hasan al-Basri understood *takwīr* as the sun losing its light, while Rabi' Ibn Khaitham held that the sun will be thrown into the ocean, whose water will turn to fire from its heat — and then observes that these interpretations do not contradict each other: first its light is extinguished, then it is cast down. All of them are describing stages of the same undoing.

From the Sunnah: Al-Bukhari recorded from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said, "The sun and the moon will be rolled up on the Day of Judgement" — Ibn Kathir notes that Al-Bukhari was alone in recording this hadith with this wording. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the Musnad of Bazzar carries the addition that they will be thrown into Hell, and reconciles the reports: since the seas themselves will have become fire and been made part of Hell (see ayah 6), to say the sun is thrown into the ocean and to say it is thrown into Hell come to the same thing.

## Ayah 2 — the stars poured out

*Inkadarat*: Ibn Kathir explains that the root of *inkidār* is *insibāb* — "to be poured out." The stars will not simply flicker off; they will spill from their places and scatter, as Allah says elsewhere, "And when the stars have fallen and scattered" (82:2). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that the righteous predecessors interpreted the word as "to fall," and that the stars will fall into the oceans. The picture is of the night sky emptied like a vessel tipped over.

## Ayah 3 — the mountains set moving

"And when the mountains are made to pass away" — Ibn Kathir: they will not remain in their places; they will be destroyed, "then the earth will be left as a flat, level plain." Mountains are the Qur'an's standing image of permanence. Here even they are put in motion and erased.

## Ayah 4 — the she-camel no one comes for

This ayah speaks the language of its first hearers with devastating precision. The *'ishār* (singular *'usharā'*) are she-camels in the tenth month of pregnancy. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the Arabs considered such a camel their most valuable asset — she promised both a new camel and abundant milk — so they guarded her and never left her loose. Ibn Kathir gathers the early explanations: Mujahid said *'uttilat* means "abandoned and left"; Ubayy bin Ka'b and Ad-Dahhak said their owners will neglect them; Ar-Rabi' bin Khuthaym said, "They will not be milked or tied up. Their masters will leave them abandoned."

Why? Ibn Kathir answers: the people will be too overwhelmed to tend to her, care for her, or benefit from her, "after she used to be the most important thing to them" — because of the great, terrifying situation that has suddenly overtaken them. On that Day, the most treasured possession a person owns will not be worth turning around for. Every reader can substitute whatever their own '*ushará'* is.

## Ayah 5 — even the wild beasts gathered

The wild animals — creatures that flee from humans and from each other — will be herded together. Ibn Kathir connects this to Allah's words: "There is not a moving creature on earth, nor a bird that flies with its two wings, but are communities like you… then unto their Lord they shall be gathered" (6:38). Ibn 'Abbas said — as recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim — "Everything will be gathered, even the flies." Nothing that lives is outside the summons.

## Ayah 6 — the seas set ablaze

*Sujjirat*: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the word carries three senses — "to set ablaze" (the interpretation Ibn 'Abbas gave in this context), "to fill," and "to mix" — and that none contradicts the others. Citing Mazhari, it lays out the sequence: first the sweet and salt waters mix and the rivers pour into the sea; then the seas merge into one swollen ocean; then that ocean is set on fire; then the sun, moon and stars are cast into it, until all the water becomes fire and is made part of Hell.

Ibn Kathir relates a striking exchange recorded by Ibn Jarir from Sa'id bin Al-Musayyib: 'Ali asked a Jewish man, "Where is the Hell?" The man said, "The sea." 'Ali said, "I think he is truthful," and recited "And by the seas kindled" (52:6) together with this ayah.

## The six signs as one unfolding scene

Ibn Kathir preserves a narration — in which Ar-Rabi' bin Anas reported from Abu Al-'Aliyah, who reported from Ubayy bin Ka'b, and which Ibn Jarir recorded with this wording — that stitches ayat 1–6 into a single narrative: "Six signs will take place before the Day of Judgement. The people will be in their marketplaces when the sun's light will go away. When they are in that situation, the stars will be scattered. When they are in that situation, the mountains will fall down upon the face of the earth, and the earth will move, quake and be in a state of mixed up confusion." The jinn flee in fright to the humans and the humans to the jinn; domestic beasts, birds and wild animals surge together in a wave of chaos. The jinn go to the sea to bring back news and find it a blazing fire; the earth splits with one great crack from the lowest earth to the highest heaven, and then a wind comes that kills them all.

Notice the detail that opens it: *people will be in their marketplaces*. The end does not announce itself in advance. It arrives in the middle of an ordinary trading day.

## Ayah 7 — souls sorted with their like

"And when the souls are joined with their mates." Ibn Kathir explains: every type of soul will be gathered with its peer, as Allah says, "Assemble those who did wrong, together with their companions" (37:22). Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from An-Nu'man bin Bashir that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ explained this ayah as meaning "those who are alike — every man will be with every group of people who performed the same deeds that he did," citing Allah's words about mankind being "in three groups" — the people of the right hand, the people of the left hand, and the foremost (56:7–10).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills out the picture with a report in Baihaqi, on the authority of Nu'man Ibn Bashir, that 'Umar Ibn al-Khattab said people doing similar deeds, good or bad, will be joined together: the scholars who served Islamic knowledge in one group, the devoted worshippers in another, the people of jihad together, those known for charity gathered in one place — and likewise thieves, robbers and adulterers each assembled with their own kind. (The translation in the bundle also renders the ayah as the souls being paired with their bodies at the resurrection; the commentary in both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān expounds the grouping-by-likeness meaning.)

## What the passage asks of you

The literary power of these ayat is that every clause is suspended — seven "whens" whose answer does not arrive within this passage at all, but waits, further on in the sūrah, at ayah 14: "Every person will know what he has brought." Ibn Kathir links this to "On the Day when every person will be confronted with all the good he has done, and all the evil he has done, he will wish that there were a great distance between him and his evil" (3:30).

So the passage strips away every external support in ascending intimacy: first the cosmos (sun, stars, mountains), then wealth (the she-camels), then the living world (the beasts, the seas), and finally it arrives at *you* — the soul, sorted by what it did and whom it resembled. The practical question ayah 7 leaves with the believer is simple and searching: your company on that Day is being decided now, by your deeds. Whoever you act like here is whom you will stand with there. And the Prophet's ﷺ counsel remains the door into all of it: whoever wishes to look at the Day of Judgement as if seeing it with his own eyes, let him read "When the sun is wound round" (81:1) — together with its two companion openings, "When the heaven is cleft asunder" (82:1) and "When the heaven is split asunder" (84:1).

passages.title: The buried girl questioned; each soul knows its record
passages.tafsir:
These seven ayat carry the long "when…" sentence of Sūrat at-Takwīr to its destination. Clause upon clause of that sentence falls within this very passage — *when* the buried girl is questioned, *when* the pages are laid open, *when* the sky is stripped away, *when* the Blaze is kindled and Paradise brought near — and only in ayah 14 does the sentence finally land on its answer: **"every soul will know what it has brought."** Ibn Kathir calls this last ayah "the conclusive response of the previous statements": everything before it exists for the sake of that one line. What holds ayat 8–14 together, then, is the movement toward personal reckoning — the scene narrows, step by step, to a single soul standing before its own record.

## The buried girl questioned (ayat 8–9)

At the centre of the passage stands its most piercing image. The *maw'ūdah* is, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, the girl-child buried alive: it was a common practice of the pre-Islamic age of ignorance (jāhiliyyah) that people would take the birth of a girl as a matter of shame for her father, and — in Ibn Kathir's words, due to their hatred of girls — the child would be buried in the dirt as soon as she was born. Islam abolished this barbaric practice completely.

Now notice what the Qur'an does with the scene. On the Day of Judgement it is not the killer who is put in the dock first — it is the *victim* who is questioned: "for what sin was she killed?" (ayah 9). Ibn Kathir explains that the female infant will be asked what sin she committed that caused her to be murdered, and that this will be "a means of frightening her murderer. For verily, if the one who was wronged is questioned, what does the wrongdoer think then?" If the court opens by examining the victim, the guilty party can only dread his own turn.

**Who is asked?** The scholars record two readings of the scene. The majority recite the verb as *su'ilat* — "she is questioned," as the standard text has it. But Ibn 'Abbas, in the report of 'Ali bin Abi Talhah, read the sense actively: "she will *ask*." Abu ad-Duha explained it the same way: "she will ask, meaning she will demand restitution for her blood" — and the like is reported from as-Suddi and Qatadah. On this reading the silenced infant becomes the plaintiff, rising to claim her own blood before Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the same possibilities: apparently the question will be posed to the girl herself, giving the victim the opportunity to prove her complete innocence, "and thus the perpetrators of this crime will be hauled up in the Divine Court of Justice" — though it is also possible, Maʿārif adds, that the question will be posed to the killers themselves: why did they commit infanticide?

**Why single out this one crime?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious question in its "Important Note": on a Day when *every* person will be asked all sorts of questions about his deeds, why does the Qur'an mention only this one interrogation here? The answer given is deeply moving. Carefully considered, this girl was the victim of the barbarism of her own parents — so there was no one to raise a complaint against the act, and no one to demand retaliation, especially since she was buried secretly with no evidence left. The ayah therefore signifies that on the Day of Reckoning, even those criminals will be exposed and hauled up in the Divine Court of Justice against whom there was no evidence, and for whom no one could stand up to demand justice. Allah knows best.

## From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir records two reports concerning the *maw'ūdah*.

First, Imam Ahmad recorded from 'A'ishah, from Judamah bint Wahb, the sister of 'Ukkashah, that she said she was in the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when he was with some people, and he said: "I was about to prohibit sexual relations with breastfeeding women, but then I saw that the Romans and the Persians have sexual relations with their women who breastfeed their children and it does not harm the children at all." Then they asked him about withdrawal during intercourse to prevent conception ('azl), and he said: "That is the minor infanticide, and it is the female infant buried alive (*maw'ūdah*) that will be questioned." Muslim, Ibn Majah, Abu Dawud, At-Tirmidhi and An-Nasa'i all recorded this hadith as well. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, which renders the phrase "hidden infanticide" and cites the report of Muslim from Judhamah bint Wahb, balances it with other ahadith in which the Prophet ﷺ allowed 'azl or remained silent when asked about it — a sign of permissibility. Citing Mazhari, it concludes that the permissibility is restricted to genuine needs, and that measures which permanently block a woman's ability to conceive are not permitted by the Sharī'ah under any circumstances.)

Second, the report of 'Umar bin Al-Khattab, recorded by Abdur-Razzaq: Qays bin 'Asim came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and confessed, "O Messenger of Allah! Verily, I buried some daughters of mine alive in the period of pre-Islamic ignorance." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ told him: "Free a slave for each one of them." When Qays explained that he was an owner of camels, the Prophet ﷺ said: "Then sacrifice a camel for each one of them." Even a crime this dark had a door of expiation open after Islam — mercy for the repentant, even as the ayah promises justice for the victim.

**A related ruling.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a juristic consequence from these ayat: burying infants alive or killing them is a major sin and a heinous brutality, and aborting a foetus after four months falls under the same category in the Sharī'ah, because within four months the foetus receives the soul and is treated as a living human being. Abortion before four months is also unlawful except in cases of necessity, though it is a sin of a lesser degree, since it does not clearly amount to the killing of a living human being.

## The pages laid open (ayah 10)

From the exposure of hidden crimes the passage turns to the exposure of every deed: the *ṣuḥuf* — the pages, the records of deeds — are laid open. Ad-Dahhak said: "Every person will be given his paper in his right hand or in his left hand." But it is Qatadah's comment, preserved by Ibn Kathir, that turns the ayah into a direct address: "O Son of Adam! It (your paper) is written in, then it is rolled up, then it will be distributed to you on the Day of Judgement. So let each man look at what he himself dictated to be written in his paper." The record is not someone else's account of you — you are its author, dictating a line with every deed, and on that Day the scroll is simply unrolled and handed back.

## Sky stripped, Fire kindled, Paradise brought near (ayat 11–13)

The final three "when" clauses complete the scene. In ayah 11 the sky is *kushiṭat*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the word comes from *kasht*, which literally means to strip the skin off an animal — a startlingly physical image: the familiar heaven flayed away like a hide. Mujahid said it "draws away"; as-Suddi said "stripped off"; and some commentators, Maʿārif notes, take *kasht* in the sense of "folding up." Maʿārif adds that this will probably occur at the first blowing of the Horn, when the stars, sun and moon that contributed to the beauty of the sky will lose their light and lustre, and the whole outlook of the sky will be changed.

Then the two destinations are unveiled together: in ayah 12 the Blaze (*al-Jaḥīm*) is *su''irat* — fiercely kindled; as-Suddi said, "it is heated." And in ayah 13 Paradise is *uzlifat* — brought near; Ad-Dahhak, Abu Malik, Qatadah and Ar-Rabi' bin Khuthaym all said this means it will be brought near *to its inhabitants*. Nothing remains at a distance. Both abodes stand in view, waiting.

## The answer: each soul knows its record (ayah 14)

And then the long sentence resolves: "every soul will know what it has brought." Ibn Kathir explains: this is the conclusive response of the previous statements — when these matters occur, every soul will know what it has done, and that will be brought forth for it — and he ties the ayah to two of its Qur'anic sisters: "On the Day when every person will be confronted with all the good he has done, and all the evil he has done, he will wish that there were a great distance between him and his evil" (3:30), and "On that Day man will be informed of what he sent forward, and what he left behind" (75:13). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that "what it has brought" means one's good and bad deeds, all of which will be in front of him — either in the form of the Record of Deeds given in his hands, or, as is understood from certain traditions, his deeds assuming a specific bodily shape. Allah knows best.

Read this way, the passage asks two things of the believer. First, to remember Qatadah's warning: the ledger being written now is one's own dictation, so let each of us look to what we are dictating into the page that will be handed back on that Day. And second, to take to heart what the buried girl's case signifies: on the Day of Reckoning, even those wrongdoers will be exposed and brought before the Divine Court of Justice against whom there was no evidence and no one to demand justice — and, in Ibn Kathir's words, if the one who was wronged is questioned, what does the wrongdoer think then?

passages.title: Oaths affirming the Quran's angelic bearer
passages.tafsir:
## From the end of the world to the source of the Word

After the sūrah's opening portrait of the Day of Resurrection — what Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls its "horrors" — and the accountability of deeds, the passage pivots. Having shown *what is coming*, Allah now swears a majestic sequence of oaths to establish *how we know*: the Qur'an that announces all of this is the truth sent down, carried by a noble, mighty, trusted angelic messenger. Ayat 15–18 are the oath; ayat 19–21 are what the oath affirms — one sentence of divine testimony: by the receding stars, by the night, by the dawn, *this is truly the word brought by a most honourable messenger*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān captures the logic of the transition: having described the horrors of Resurrection and the accountability of deeds, Allah swears by the stars to confirm that the Qur'an is truth sent down, fully protected from any interruption or distortion — and that the angel who descended with it was known to the Prophet ﷺ beforehand — so there can be no room for doubt about its veracity.

## The oath by the vanishing stars (ayat 15–16)

The oath opens with two mysterious words: *al-khunnas* (ayah 15), the ones that recede or withdraw, and *al-jawār al-kunnas* (ayah 16), the ones that travel and hide. Ibn Kathir records — through Ibn Jarir, from Khalid bin 'Ar'arah — that 'Ali was asked about these ayat and answered: "These are the stars that withdraw (disappear) during the day and sweep across the sky (appear) at night." The stars are always there, but daylight hides them; night reveals them again as they sweep across the sky.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a fascinating layer: these verses swear by five stars the ancient Greeks called *khamsah mutaḥayyirah*, "the five wandering stars," because they seem to stray irregularly across the sky — sometimes moving east to west, sometimes west to east. The Greeks offered contradictory explanations for this strange motion, and the research of modern scientists concurs with some of the ancient philosophers and differs from others. Maʿārif draws a pointed lesson from the Qur'an's restraint here: the Creator alone knows the truth and reality — the scientists merely guess and conjecture — and the Qur'an deliberately did not involve its readers in such a debate. Instead, Allah directed us to what is beneficial: to observe His omnipotence and consummate wisdom in these wheeling lights, and to repose our faith in Him.

**These ayat in the Prophet's ﷺ own recitation.** Muslim recorded in his Sahih, and An-Nasa'i in his Book of Tafsir, from 'Amr bin Hurayth: "I prayed the Morning prayer behind the Prophet ﷺ, and I heard him reciting: *But nay! I swear by al-Khunnas, al-Jawār al-Kunnas, and by the night when it 'as'as, and by the day when it tanaffas.*" There is something fitting in the scene itself — these oaths by fading stars and breaking dawn, recited aloud at the very hour when the stars are receding and the dawn is arriving.

## Night departing, dawn arriving (ayat 17–18)

Ayah 17 swears by the night "when it *'as'as*" — and here the early scholars genuinely differed, because the Arabic word carries two opposite senses. One group understood it as the night **advancing**: Mujahid said "its darkening," Sa'id bin Jubayr said "when it begins," and al-Hasan al-Basri said "when it covers the people," a view shared by 'Atiyah al-'Awfi. Another group understood it as the night **departing**: Ibn 'Abbas — as reported by both 'Ali bin Abi Talhah and al-'Awfi — said "when it goes away," and Mujahid, Qatadah, ad-Dahhak, Zayd bin Aslam and his son 'Abdur-Rahman said the same.

Ibn Kathir weighs in personally: he inclines to the meaning of approaching, since it is as if Allah is swearing by the night and its darkness as it draws on, and by the morning and its light as it shines from the east — matching the paired oaths elsewhere in the Qur'an: "By the night as it envelops. By the day as it appears in brightness" (92:1–2) and "By the forenoon. By the night when it darkens" (93:1–2). Yet he also notes that many scholars of the fundamentals of the language held that *'as'as* genuinely means both advancing and retreating — one word bearing both motions — so, he concludes, it is correct that both could be intended, and Allah knows best. The ambiguity is almost the point: the oath holds the whole turning of night, its arrival and its retreat, in a single word.

Ayah 18 answers it with the dawn "when it *tanaffas*." Ad-Dahhak explained it as "when it rises"; Qatadah as "when it brightens and advances" — morning light spreading and gaining strength.

## The answer of the oath: a most honourable messenger (ayah 19)

All of this — the hiding stars, the ebbing night, the swelling dawn — is sworn for one declaration: "Indeed, this Qur'an is surely the word of a noble messenger" (ayah 19). Ibn Kathir explains: the Qur'an is being conveyed by a noble messenger, meaning an honourable angel of good character and radiant appearance — **Jibril**. This identification is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, ash-Sha'bi, Maymun bin Mihran, al-Hasan, Qatadah, ar-Rabi' bin Anas, ad-Dahhak and others.

Calling the Qur'an the "word" of Jibril does not mean he authored it; it means he is the one *delivering* it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why "messenger" (*rasūl*) fits an angel: the word is used for angels just as it is used for prophets, and all three qualities attributed to this messenger in the following verses are truly present in Jibril, peace be upon him. Maʿārif also notes honestly that some commentators took "honourable messenger" to refer to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself and accordingly attempted to read the three qualities as describing him.

## The qualities of the carrier (ayat 20–21)

Why describe the angel at all? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayat 20–21 as attributing three qualities to this noble messenger: he possesses power; he has high status and lofty rank with Allah and is obeyed in the upper realm; and he is trusted.

**"Full of power" (*dhī quwwah*, ayah 20).** Ibn Kathir links this to Allah's description in Sūrah an-Najm, "He has been taught by one mighty in power" (53:5–6) — mighty in creation, mighty in strength, mighty in actions.

**"Held in honour by the Lord of the Throne" (*makīn*, ayah 20).** He has high status and lofty rank with Allah Himself.

**"Obeyed there, and trustworthy" (*muṭāʿ thamma amīn*, ayah 21).** Ibn Kathir: he has prestige, his word is listened to, and he is obeyed among the most high gathering of angels. Qatadah said: "This means in the heavens. He is not one of the lower ranking (ordinary) angels. Rather he is from the high ranking, prestigious angels. He is respected and has been chosen for (the delivery of) this magnificent Message." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to the account of the Miʿrāj as evidence of his being obeyed: when Jibril accompanied the Prophet ﷺ through the heavens and ordered the angels appointed over their doors to open them, they obeyed him. And finally *amīn* — trustworthy: as Maʿārif puts it, there is no possibility of his committing any breach of trust or tampering with the message he conveys. Ibn Kathir adds that this is something very great: the Almighty Lord Himself has commended His servant and angelic Messenger, Jibril — just as He has commended His servant and human Messenger, Muhammad ﷺ, in the ayah that follows.

## What the passage asks of the reader

The Book you hold is vouched for by its Sender and carried by a bearer whom Allah Himself describes: strong, stationed in honour with the Lord of the Throne, obeyed in the heavens, and utterly trustworthy — one who, in Maʿārif's words, could commit no breach of trust or tampering with what he conveys. That is why, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, there can be no room for doubt about the Qur'an's veracity: it is truth sent down, fully protected from any interruption or distortion. And the oaths that open the passage are not decoration: the same Allah whose stars wander in courses whose reality the Creator alone knows, who turns the night and brightens the dawn, is the One calling these signs to witness for His Book — directing us not to fruitless speculation, but to observe His omnipotence and consummate wisdom and to repose our faith in Him. The believer who watches stars fade at Fajr — the very hour the Prophet ﷺ recited these ayat — stands inside the scene of the oath itself.

passages.title: The Prophet vindicated against madness and devilry
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the Qur'an's own character reference for the man who brought it. Having sworn a series of oaths and declared that the Qur'an "is surely the word of a noble messenger" — the angel Jibra'il — in ayat 19–21, the surah now turns to the human messenger, Muhammad ﷺ, and answers the accusations Makkah was hurling at him one by one: he is not mad (ayah 22), he genuinely saw the angel who brings him revelation (ayah 23), he holds nothing of it back (ayah 24), and what he recites is not the whispering of a devil (ayah 25). Then comes the devastating question that closes the case: "So what other path would you take?" (ayah 26). What binds these five ayat together is a single argument: the revelation is sound at every link of its chain — sound in its angelic carrier, sound in its human recipient, and untouchable by any devil.

## Two messengers, one commendation

Ibn Kathir draws attention to something remarkable in the flow of these ayat. In ayat 19–21 Allah praised Jibra'il — powerful, of high rank with the Lord of the Throne, obeyed among the angels, trustworthy. Then, in ayah 22, He turns and praises Muhammad ﷺ in the same breath. Ibn Kathir calls this "something very great": that the Almighty Lord has commended His servant and angelic messenger, Jibril, just as He has commended His servant and human Messenger, Muhammad ﷺ. The Qur'an's reliability rests on both figures, and Allah Himself vouches for both.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the qualities of the angelic carrier that set up this passage: Jibra'il possesses power, holds a lofty rank with Allah and is obeyed in the upper realm, and is trusted — "there is no possibility of his committing any breach of trust or tampering with the message he conveys." It notes that his being obeyed by the other angels is established through the hadith of the Miʿrāj: when he accompanied the Prophet ﷺ through the heavens and ordered the angels at their gates to open them, they obeyed. With the carrier's integrity established, the surah turns to the recipient.

## Ayah 22: "Your companion is not insane"

The Quraysh had explained away the revelation with the crudest slander available: the man is majnūn, possessed, mad. Ayah 22 flatly denies it — and notice how it names him. Not "the Prophet," not even "Muhammad," but ṣāḥibukum, "your companion," "your fellow man." The commentators Ash-Shaʿbi, Maymun bin Mihran, Abu Salih and others confirm, as Ibn Kathir records, that this refers to Muhammad ﷺ. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the ayah simply as a rebuttal to the foolish criticism of the enemies who said — far be it from him! — that Muhammad ﷺ is insane. The argument is addressed to people who knew him: this is your own companion, the man who has lived among you.

## Ayah 23: the sighting on the clear horizon

The proof that he is not deluded follows at once: "And he did see that angel on the clear horizon." Ibn Kathir explains that Muhammad ﷺ saw Jibra'il — the very messenger who brings him revelation from Allah — in the form Allah created him in, his true angelic form, and he had six hundred wings.

Ibn Kathir identifies this as the first sighting, which took place at al-Batha' in Makkah, and connects it to Surah an-Najm: "He has been taught by one mighty in power... while he was in the highest part of the horizon. Then he approached and came closer, and was at a distance of two bows' length or less" (53:5–10). A second sighting of Jibra'il in his true form occurred at the Lote Tree of the utmost boundary, Sidrat al-Muntaha (53:13–16). From this Ibn Kathir draws a careful historical inference: since Surah at-Takwir mentions only the first sighting, it seems apparent — and Allah knows best — that it was revealed before the Night Journey (al-Isra'), while Surah an-Najm, which mentions the second sighting, was revealed after it.

Why does the Qur'an cite this vision here? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the purpose plainly: to show that the Prophet ﷺ was well-acquainted with Jibra'il, the angel of revelation. He had seen him in his original shape. "Therefore, there can be no room for doubt in the veracity of revelation he brings to him."

## Ayah 24: two readings, one integrity

Ayah 24 — "and he does not withhold what is revealed to him of the unseen" — carries a fascinating feature of the Qur'an's transmission: it has been recited in two authentic ways, differing in a single letter.

One recitation reads ẓanīn (with the letter ẓāʼ): the Prophet ﷺ is not "suspect" over the Unseen — as Ibn Kathir glosses it, he is not following false conjecture about what Allah revealed. The other reads ḍanīn (with the letter ḍād): he is not stingy with the Unseen — he does not hoard the revelation but conveys it to everyone. Sufyan bin 'Uyaynah said the two readings converge on the same essential meaning: "They mean that he is not a liar, nor is he a wicked, sinful person. The ẓanīn is one who follows false supposition, and the ḍanīn is one who is stingy."

Qatadah captured the second sense beautifully: "The Qur'an was unseen and Allah revealed it to Muhammad ﷺ, and he did not withhold it from the people. Rather he announced it, conveyed it, and offered it to everyone who wanted it." 'Ikrimah and Ibn Zayd said the same, and Ibn Jarir preferred the reading ḍanīn. Ibn Kathir's own verdict is generous to both: each recitation has been confirmed by numerous routes of transmission, and the meaning is correct either way. Read together, the two recitations give a complete portrait of the trustworthy transmitter: he neither adds by guesswork nor subtracts by withholding. The revelation passes through him whole.

## Ayah 25: not the word of an outcast devil

Having ruled out madness, the surah rules out the other slander: that the Qur'an is the dictation of a shayṭān rajīm — an outcast, stoned devil driven from the heavens. Ibn Kathir's explanation is twofold: a devil is not able to produce this Qur'an, nor would it even befit him to do so. He points to the parallel passage: "And it is not the devils who have brought it down. Neither would it suit them, nor can they. Verily, they have been removed far from hearing it" (26:210–212).

## Ayah 26: "So what other path would you take?"

Then comes the question that ends the argument: fa-ayna tadhhabūn — "then where are you going?" Ibn Kathir unpacks its force: where has your reason gone, that you reject this Qur'an when it is manifest, clear, and evident that it is the truth from Allah? Qatadah read it as a question of direction in life itself: where are you going — away from the Book of Allah and His obedience?

Ibn Kathir illustrates the point with a scene from after the Prophet's ﷺ time. When the delegation of Banu Hanifah came to Abu Bakr as-Siddiq as Muslims, he asked them to recite something, and they recited from the so-called "Qur'an" of Musaylimah the Liar — total gibberish, terribly poor in style. Abu Bakr's response echoes this very ayah: "Woe unto you! Where have your senses gone? By Allah, this speech did not come from a god."

## Hearing the passage whole

Ayat 22–26 clear the channel of revelation from top to bottom. The angel who carries it is mighty, highly placed, obeyed, and trustworthy; the man who receives it is sane, an eyewitness of that angel, and utterly faithful in passing on every word; and the source can be no devil, for a devil can neither produce such speech nor would it befit him. The truth of this Book being manifest, clear, and evident, the passage leaves each listener standing before its closing question, the same one Abu Bakr would later turn on the reciters of gibberish: if you walk away from this Book, where exactly are you going?

passages.title: A reminder for all, willed only through Allah
passages.tafsir:
# A Reminder for All — If Allah Wills (81:27–29)

These three ayat are the closing words of Sūrah at-Takwīr. The verses immediately before them have been defending the Qur'an's origin: it is the word brought by a most honorable messenger — the angel Jibril, mighty, trusted, and obeyed among the angels — the Prophet ﷺ is no madman, and it is not the word of the outcast Shaytan. Having established where the Qur'an came *from*, Allah now states, in a single breath, what this Book *is*, who it is *for*, and where the power to respond to it ultimately *comes from*. What binds the three ayat together is a deliberate movement: from the Qur'an (ayah 27), to the human being who chooses (ayah 28), to Allah whose will encompasses every choice (ayah 29).

## Ayah 27 — a reminder for all the worlds

*"Surely this Qur'an is only a reminder (dhikr) to the whole world."* Ibn Kathir's comment is brief and complete: this Qur'an is a reminder for all of mankind — "they are reminded by it and receive admonition from it." Two things stand out.

**It is a *reminder*.** The word *dhikr* — remembrance, reminder — frames the Qur'an not as entertainment or ornament but as admonition: something people are meant to be awakened and corrected by. The sūrah has just spent verse after verse establishing where the Qur'an came *from*; now it says what the Qur'an came *to do*.

**It is for *al-ʿālamīn* — all the worlds.** Not for one tribe, one city, or one generation. The reminder is set before all of mankind; whoever hears it is among those it addresses.

## Ayah 28 — for whoever wills to walk straight

*"To whoever of you wills to take the Straight Way."* The universal reminder now narrows to the individual. The Book is offered to everyone, but it benefits the one who *wills* — who actually wants to walk straight.

Ibn Kathir draws the practical conclusion with striking firmness: whoever seeks guidance "must adhere to this Qur'an, for verily it is his salvation and guidance. **There is no guidance in other than it.**" This is the living edge of the ayah. Wanting to be upright is not a mood; it has an address. The person who sincerely wills to walk straight is being told exactly where that road runs — through this Book — and told that no substitute exists.

Notice also the honesty of the wording: *"whoever of you wills."* The Qur'an does not pretend that everyone will respond. It sets the reminder before all the worlds and then respects the reality that human beings genuinely choose.

## Ayah 29 — and no one wills except that Allah wills

Then comes the correction that guards the whole matter from arrogance. *"But you cannot will to do so, except by the Will of Allah, the Lord of all the worlds."*

Ibn Kathir records a report from Sulayman bin Musa about the occasion behind this verse: when ayah 28 was revealed — "to whomsoever among you who wills to walk straight" — **Abu Jahl** seized on it and said, "The matter is up to us. If we wish, we will stand straight, and we do not wish, we will not stand straight." So Allah revealed ayah 29: *"And you cannot will unless Allah wills — the Lord of all that exists."*

Abu Jahl's boast is the permanent temptation of the human ego: to hear "whoever wills" and conclude that guidance is our own achievement, held entirely in our own hands. Ayah 29 closes that door. As Ibn Kathir explains: the will has not been left to creatures such that whoever wishes guidance simply guides himself and whoever wishes misguidance simply strays on his own — rather, all of it happens according to the will of Allah, the Exalted, and He is the Lord of all that exists.

This is the balanced creed of Ahl al-Sunnah as these two verses themselves teach it. Ayah 28 affirms that you truly *do* will — your choice is real, and you are addressed and accountable through it. Ayah 29 affirms that your will operates *inside* Allah's will, never outside it or independent of it. Neither verse cancels the other; together they cancel both errors — the fatalism that says human choice means nothing, and the self-sufficiency of Abu Jahl that says it means everything. And the ayah seals the point with the divine name that explains it: He is *Rabb al-ʿālamīn*, Lord of all the worlds — the same "worlds" to whom the reminder was sent in ayah 27. The One who sent the Book to all creation is the same One who sustains and governs every heart that receives it.

## Living the passage

The sūrah — which Ibn Kathir considered, on the evidence of its verses and with the caution "and Allah knows best," to have been revealed before the Night Journey (al-Isrāʾ) — thus ends by placing the reader personally at a fork. The reminder has reached you; that part is done. What remains is your willing — turn to this Qur'an, for there is no guidance elsewhere — joined to the humility of knowing that even that turning happens only by the will of the Lord of all the worlds, never as a feat to boast of. The believer therefore strives as one whose choice matters, and prays as one whose choice depends entirely on Allah.

And with this ayah, as Ibn Kathir writes, ends the tafsir of Sūrah at-Takwīr — "and all praise and thanks are due to Allah."
